stem: Steepest-ascent hill climbing always finds the global maximum.
solutionSteps: It stops at the first peak where no neighbour is better: possibly a local maximum.
takeaway: Restart or use SA/GA to escape.
source: Lecture 3, slide 14-16
why: It stops at the first peak where no neighbour is better: possibly a local maximum.

stem: In hill climbing, what happens if the best neighbour's value equals the current value?
takeaway: Pseudocode Fig 4.2.
source: Lecture 3, slide 16
options: The algorithm returns the current state

whyWrong.B: That's not steepest ascent.
whyWrong.C: Moves only if strictly better (VALUE(neighbor) ≤ VALUE(current) → return).
whyWrong.D: No restart in the basic algorithm.

stem: Select ALL true statements about hill climbing (Lecture 3). (Select ALL that apply.)
takeaway: One state, greedy moves.
source: Lecture 3, slide 14-16
options: It keeps track of one current state
It needs a population of candidates
It accepts worse moves with probability e^(−Δ/T)
It moves to the neighbour with the highest value (steepest ascent)

stem: In simulated annealing, a neighbour is worse by Δ = 2 at T = 5. Acceptance probability?
takeaway: p = exp(−Δ/T).

stem: As the temperature T decreases, simulated annealing becomes MORE likely to accept worse moves.
solutionSteps: Lower T → exp(−Δ/T) smaller → fewer worse moves accepted.
takeaway: High T explores; low T is selective.
source: Lecture 3, slide 23
why: Lower T → exp(−Δ/T) smaller → fewer worse moves accepted.

stem: Match each SA limitation to its consequence.
solutionSteps: Cooling too fast → may behave like hill climbing and get trapped early
Cooling too slow → may require many iterations before convergence
Parameter sensitivity → initial temperature and schedule must be chosen carefully
Randomness → different runs may return different solutions
takeaway: SA can escape local optima but guarantees nothing in one run.
source: Lecture 3, slide 28
right: different runs may return different solutions
may require many iterations before convergence
guaranteed global optimum in one run
initial temperature and schedule must be chosen carefully

stem: In tournament selection, a larger tournament size k increases diversity in the population.
solutionSteps: Larger k → higher selection pressure → LESS diversity, faster convergence. Small k (2) keeps more diversity.
takeaway: k controls selection pressure.
source: Lecture 3, slide 36
why: Larger k → higher selection pressure → LESS diversity, faster convergence. Small k (2) keeps more diversity.

stem: Which local search method fits each scenario?
solutionSteps: Smooth landscape, need a quick decent answer → hill climbing
Many local optima, single candidate, can tune a cooling schedule → simulated annealing
Huge search space with many good alternatives to explore in parallel → genetic algorithm
takeaway: HC fast, SA escapes optima, GA explores populations.
source: Lecture 3, slide 14-41
left: Smooth landscape, need a quick decent answer
Many local optima, single candidate, can tune a cooling schedule
Huge search space with many good alternatives to explore in parallel

stem: Simulated annealing (minimising energy). A neighbour is worse by Δ = 9 at temperature T = 5. Give (1) the acceptance probability p = exp(−Δ/T) (4 dp) and (2) whether the move is accepted if the random number is r = 0.079 (accept if r < p): answer Yes or No.
solutionSteps: r = 0.079 < p → accept the worse move.
takeaway: High T → p near 1 (explore). Low T → p near 0 (behaves like hill climbing). Better moves are always accepted.
source: Lecture 3 (Local search: hill climbing, simulated annealing, genetic algorithm)

stem: In the 8-queens formulation (Lecture 3), state x = (8, 8, 8, 2, 8, 5, 3, 8) gives the row of the queen in each column 1..8. The cost is the number of pairs of queens attacking each other (same row or same diagonal). What is the cost?
solutionSteps: Check every pair of columns (i, j): attack if xᵢ = xⱼ or |xᵢ − xⱼ| = j − i.

Attacking pairs: (1,2) same row; (1,3) same row; (1,5) same row; (1,8) same row; (2,3) same row; (2,5) same row; (2,7) diagonal; (2,8) same row; (3,5) same row; (3,6) diagonal; (3,8) same row; (5,8) same row.
takeaway: Each 8-queens state has 8×7 = 56 successors (move one queen within its column).
source: Lecture 3 (Local search: hill climbing, simulated annealing, genetic algorithm)

Attacking pairs: (1,5) same row; (1,6) diagonal; (2,3) same row; (2,4) diagonal; (2,7) diagonal; (4,7) diagonal; (4,8) same row.
takeaway: Each 8-queens state has 8×7 = 56 successors (move one queen within its column).
source: Lecture 3 (Local search: hill climbing, simulated annealing, genetic algorithm)

takeaway: Hill climbing stops at a peak, which may only be a LOCAL maximum.
source: Lecture 3 (Local search: hill climbing, simulated annealing, genetic algorithm)
